items.reason: Ten agreement errors: who works→work; have increased→has increased (the number is singular); There is→There are; technology allow→allows; each of … offer→offers; managers believes→believe; productivity fall→falls; staff is→staff are; advantages … outweighs→outweigh; this trend are→is.

chapters.title: 2. Tense Mastery & Time Precision (1/2)
chapters.group: Module 1 · The Foundational Zero-to-Hero Grammar Engine
blocks: The twelve tenses mapped, the five that IELTS rewards, and the two critical pairs (past simple vs present perfect, present simple vs present continuous) that cause almost all tense errors.

Subject-verb agreement made your verbs match. Tense makes them sit in the right time. In IELTS this is not a small point of grammar; it is a matter of meaning. Writing Task 1 describes data that already happened or is happening now, Task 2 predicts and generalises, and Speaking moves constantly between past stories and future plans. Put a verb in the wrong time and you have not just made a grammar slip, you have said something untrue about when it happened. That is why examiners treat tense control as a core signal of the Band 6-to-7 jump.
2.1 What a tense actually is (zero assumption)
An English tense carries two pieces of information at once:
Time: past, present, or future. (When did it happen?)
Aspect: simple, continuous, perfect, or perfect continuous. (Is it a whole finished event, an action in progress, an action linked to another time, or a mix?)

Three times multiplied by four aspects gives the twelve tenses. That sounds like a lot, but the good news for IELTS is that five of them do about 90 per cent of the work, and this chapter foregrounds those five while still showing you the full map so nothing is a mystery.
The four aspects, in plain words:
a whole event, a fact, a habit
an action linked to a later time; “before now / before then”
an action in progress up to a point, with duration
2.2 The complete map of the twelve tenses
Study the whole table once so you can recognise every form. Then move to 2.3, where we foreground the five that matter most.
past action still relevant; trend up to now
duration of an action continuing to now
Prices have been rising for a decade.
finished event at a finished time
action in progress at a past moment
Sales were falling when the law changed.
an earlier past action before another past action
duration up to a point in the past
It had been raining for hours before it stopped.
Demand will rise over the next decade.
action in progress at a future moment
By 2030, most cars will be running on electricity.
an action completed before a future point
By 2040, the city will have doubled in size.
duration up to a future point
By June she will have been working here for ten years.

p.p. = past participle (the third form: go / went / gone; rise / rose / risen). The high-frequency irregular list is in Appendix A at the back of the book. Learn it as fixed items, the way you learned vocabulary.
2.3 The five tenses IELTS actually rewards
You can describe any graph and answer any Speaking question accurately with these five. Master them before you worry about the rest.
Present simple for facts, habits, general truths, and Task 2 positions.
Present continuous for what is happening now and for current trends.
Past simple for finished events and historical graph data.
Present perfect for actions and trends that reach up to the present.
Future (will / going to) for predictions and plans.
Two pairs inside this five cause almost all tense errors. The rest of the chapter drills those two pairs, because fixing them fixes most of your tense marks.

chapters.title: 2. Tense Mastery & Time Precision (2/2)
chapters.group: Module 1 · The Foundational Zero-to-Hero Grammar Engine
blocks: 2.4 Critical pair 1 · Past simple versus present perfect
This is the single most common tense confusion for Bangladeshi candidates, and it is decisive in Task 1.
Use the past simple when the time is finished, and often stated: in 2010, last year, two decades ago, between 2000 and 2010.
Use the present perfect when the action reaches up to now, or when the exact time does not matter: signalled by since, for, over the past decade, recently, so far, already.
Past simple: The population rose in 2010. (a finished year) / Present perfect: The population has risen since 2010. (2010 up to the present)
The clearest signal is the time word:
Signals PRESENT PERFECT (time up to now)
so far, up to now, already, lately
The company has launched its first product in 2009.
The company launched its first product in 2009.
Since 2020, remote work became far more common.
Since 2020, remote work has become far more common.

In Bangla, “আমি দেখেছিলাম” and “আমি দেখেছি” can sound almost the same, so let the time words decide: a specific finished time (in 2010, last year, ago) takes the past simple; since, for or recently takes the present perfect.

Data tied to a past year is past simple; a trend running to the present is present perfect.

Skills: Writing
Task 1: Sales fell in 2015 but have recovered every year since.
2.5 Critical pair 2 · Present simple versus present continuous
Use the present simple for a permanent fact, a habit, or a general truth. This is the tense of most Task 2 topic sentences and of process descriptions.
Use the present continuous for something happening right now or a temporary current trend, especially with words such as currently, at the moment, these days, nowadays.
Present simple (general truth): Governments spend public money on healthcare. / Present continuous (current trend): The number of remote workers is increasing steadily.
Task 2 general truth: Many people believe that university education should be free. / Task 1 current trend: Demand for electric vehicles is rising sharply at present.
2.6 Future forms · will, going to, and the present continuous
Three forms cover the future in IELTS:
will + base verb: predictions, general future facts, and decisions made at the moment of speaking. If this trend continues, sea levels will rise further.
be going to + base verb: plans already decided, and predictions based on present evidence. The government is going to introduce a carbon tax next year.
present continuous: fixed personal arrangements (mostly Speaking). I am meeting my supervisor tomorrow.
For Task 1 projections (a graph that forecasts into the future) and Task 2 consequences, will is the workhorse: Unless emissions are cut, the planet will face irreversible damage.
2.7 The perfect and continuous tenses you should at least recognise
You will not need all twelve constantly, but recognising them lets you read a prompt correctly and adds range when it is natural.
Past perfect (had + p.p.) shows which of two past events came first. Useful in Speaking Part 2 narratives. By the time the report was published, the situation had already changed.
Present perfect continuous (have been + -ing) stresses the duration of a trend reaching now. House prices have been rising steadily for over a decade.
Future perfect (will have + p.p.) projects a completed change by a future point, strong in Task 1 forecasts. By 2040, the population will have doubled.
Use these for genuine range, not decoration. One accurate past perfect in a Speaking narrative shows control; a forced one that does not fit reads as an error.
Two continuous-tense errors dominate Bangladeshi scripts. Both come from over-using the -ing form, partly because Bangla uses its continuous form more freely than English does.

Error type 1 · Stative verbs cannot be continuous. Some verbs describe a state, not an action in progress: know, believe, understand, mean, agree, want, need, prefer, like, love, hate, seem, appear, belong, own, contain, consist, depend, and have when it means possession.
✗ I am knowing the answer. / He is having two cars. / I am understanding your point now.
✓ I know the answer. / He has two cars. / I understand your point now.

Error type 2 · “Since” and “for” take the perfect, not the present continuous. A trend that started in the past and continues now uses the present perfect or present perfect continuous, never the plain present continuous.
✗ The population is increasing since 2010. / Prices are rising for the last five years.
✓ The population has increased / has been increasing since 2010. / Prices have been rising for the last five years.
Time frames win or lose Task 1

In Writing Task 1, tense is not optional accuracy; it is the backbone of the answer. A chart with a past date range must stay in the past simple throughout. A trend that reaches the present takes the present perfect. A graph with a future projection takes will or is expected to. In Task 2, general truths and your own position sit in the present simple, while consequences and predictions take the future.

Skills: Writing, Speaking
Task 1: Car sales peaked in 2015, have fallen every year since, and are expected to stabilise after 2025.
Task 2: Because cities continue to expand, housing shortages will worsen unless governments act now.
Speaking Part 3: Attitudes have changed a great deal recently, and I think they will keep changing.
End of Chapter 2. Chapter 3 (Articles & Noun Types) follows.

chapters.title: 2. Practice · Tense Mastery & Time Precision
chapters.group: Module 1 · The Foundational Zero-to-Hero Grammar Engine
blocks: Of the twelve English tenses, only five do almost all the work in IELTS: present simple, present continuous, past simple, present perfect, and future forms. Master these five before worrying about the rest.
**Why it matters:** You can describe any graph and answer almost any Speaking question accurately with just five tenses.
**Present simple** -- facts, habits, general truths, Task 2 positions.
**Present continuous** -- what's happening now, current trends.
**Past simple** -- finished events, historical graph data.
**Present perfect** -- actions or trends that reach up to now.

Two pairs inside this five cause almost all tense errors in Bangladeshi candidates' writing -- past simple vs present perfect, and present simple vs present continuous. Fixing those two pairs fixes most of your tense marks.

blocks.title: Exercise 2.1 · Tense Selection
blocks.instructions: Put the verb in brackets into the correct tense. Each item has one best answer determined by its time signal or meaning.

items.prompt: In 2008, the company (open) ______ its first overseas office.
items.answer: opened
accepted: opened
items.reason: Finished year (2008), past simple.

items.prompt: Since 2015, the government (invest) ______ heavily in renewable energy.
items.answer: has invested
accepted: has invested
items.reason: “Since 2015” reaches to now, present perfect.

items.prompt: At the moment, the number of tourists (rise) ______ rapidly.
items.answer: is rising
accepted: is rising
items.reason: “At the moment”, present continuous.

items.prompt: Water (freeze) ______ at zero degrees Celsius.
items.answer: freezes
accepted: freezes
items.reason: General scientific truth, present simple.

items.prompt: By the time the survey ended, attitudes (already / change) ______.
items.answer: had already changed
accepted: had already changed
items.reason: An action completed before another past event, past perfect.

items.prompt: I (know) ______ the answer to that question. (correct the tense if wrong)
items.answer: know
accepted: know
items.reason: “I am knowing” is wrong; know is stative and stays simple present.

items.prompt: House prices (increase) ______ steadily for the last ten years.
items.answer: have been increasing
accepted: have been increasing
have increased
items.reason: “For the last ten years” reaches to now; present perfect continuous stresses the duration.

items.prompt: If this trend continues, the population (double) ______ by 2050.
items.answer: will double
accepted: will double
items.reason: A real future prediction, first-conditional future with “will.”

items.prompt: Last summer, the temperature (rise) ______ by three degrees.
items.answer: rose
accepted: rose
items.reason: “Last summer” is finished time, past simple.

items.prompt: Nowadays, more and more people (work) ______ from home.
items.answer: are working
accepted: are working
items.reason: “Nowadays” plus a current trend, present continuous.

items.prompt: The factory (close) ______ down in 1998 and has never reopened.
items.answer: closed
accepted: closed
items.reason: A finished event (1998), past simple.

items.prompt: Over the past decade, technology (transform) ______ the way we communicate.
items.answer: has transformed
accepted: has transformed
items.reason: “Over the past decade” reaches to now, present perfect.

items.prompt: He (have) ______ two brothers and one sister. (state, not action)
items.answer: has
accepted: has
items.reason: Possession is stative; “is having” would be wrong here.

items.prompt: Between 2000 and 2010, unemployment (fall) ______ gradually.
items.answer: fell
accepted: fell
items.reason: A finished past range (2000 to 2010), past simple.

items.prompt: Currently, the government (consider) ______ three new proposals.
items.answer: is considering
accepted: is considering
items.reason: “Currently”, present continuous.

items.prompt: She (understand) ______ the problem now, after the explanation. (correct the tense if wrong)
items.answer: understands
accepted: understands
items.reason: “Is understanding” is wrong; understand is stative, present simple.

items.prompt: By 2030, most new cars (be) ______ electric, experts predict.
items.answer: will be
accepted: will be
items.reason: A future prediction for a future point, future simple.

items.prompt: The graph shows that consumption (drop) ______ sharply in 2012.
items.answer: dropped
accepted: dropped
items.reason: Tied to a finished year (2012), past simple.

items.prompt: So far this year, exports (grow) ______ by twelve per cent.
items.answer: have grown
accepted: have grown
items.reason: “So far this year” reaches to now, present perfect.

items.prompt: Governments (spend) ______ large sums on defence every year. (general truth)
items.answer: spend
accepted: spend
items.reason: A repeated general truth (“every year”), present simple.

blocks: Past simple or present perfect? It's the single most common tense confusion in Task 1 writing. The rule is about time: finished periods take past simple, periods reaching up to now take present perfect.
**Why it matters:** This is the single most common tense confusion for Bangladeshi candidates, and it's decisive in Task 1 trend description.
Use **past simple** when the time is finished and often stated: in 2010, last year, two decades ago.
Use **present perfect** when the action reaches up to now, or the exact time doesn't matter: since, for, over the past decade, recently.
The population rose in 2010 (a finished year) vs the population has risen since 2010 (2010 up to the present).

Time words like "in 2015" or "two decades ago" call for past simple; "since 2015", "for five years", or "so far" call for present perfect. Train yourself to scan the time expression first -- it tells you the tense before you even think about the verb.

blocks.title: Exercise 2.2 · Task 1 Trend Description
blocks.instructions: Write one paragraph describing the trend, using the past simple for finished data, the present perfect for the change up to the present, and a future form for the projection. Then compare with the model.

items.prompt: Write one accurate paragraph describing the trend for “Coffee consumption per person in Country X, 1990 to 2030 (projected).” Use the past simple for finished data, the present perfect for the change up to the present (assume “now” is 2025), and a future form for the projection. Notes: 1990 low, about 2 kg; rose steadily through the 1990s; 2000 reached 5 kg; fell slightly between 2005 and 2010; has risen again every year since 2010; 2025 stands at about 8 kg; projected to reach 10 kg by 2030.
items.answer: In 1990, coffee consumption in Country X was low, at roughly 2 kilograms per person. It then rose steadily throughout the 1990s, reaching 5 kilograms by 2000. Consumption fell slightly between 2005 and 2010, but it has risen every year since, and it now stands at about 8 kilograms per person. Looking ahead, the figure is projected to reach 10 kilograms by 2030.
accepted: In 1990, coffee consumption in Country X was low, at roughly 2 kilograms per person. It then rose steadily throughout the 1990s, reaching 5 kilograms by 2000. Consumption fell slightly between 2005 and 2010, but it has risen every year since, and it now stands at about 8 kilograms per person. Looking ahead, the figure is projected to reach 10 kilograms by 2030.
items.reason: was, rose, reaching, fell = finished past data with stated years (past simple). has risen = the change reaches the present (present perfect). now stands = the present situation in 2025 (present simple). is projected to reach = a future forecast.

chapters.title: 3. Articles (A, An, The) & Noun Types
chapters.group: Module 1 · The Foundational Zero-to-Hero Grammar Engine
blocks: The single highest-error area for Bangla speakers. Countable vs uncountable nouns, the three articles plus the zero article, a four-step proofreading decision process, and the fixed cases.

If you fix only one chapter in this whole book, fix this one. Articles are the single highest-error area for learners whose first language does not have them, and Bangla, Hindi, Urdu, and Nepali all lack a direct equivalent of a / an / the. This is not a minor detail. Article errors are the number one reason that otherwise strong Band 7 candidates stay stuck at Band 6.0, because the mistakes are frequent, they appear in almost every sentence, and your ear cannot catch them: your first language never trained it to.
Whether you can use a / an at all depends on this distinction, so learn it before the article rules.
Countable nouns can be counted and have a plural form: one book, two books; a student, five students. They can take a / an in the singular.
Uncountable nouns are treated as a single mass and have no plural form and no a / an: information (never informations), water, advice.

The high-frequency uncountable nouns that trip up Bangladeshi candidates, worth memorising as a fixed block: information, advice, knowledge, research, equipment, furniture, accommodation, traffic, progress, news, money, water, work, luggage, baggage, software, staff, homework, feedback, transport, machinery, vocabulary.
To count an uncountable noun, use a partitive phrase (a unit word) plus of:
a study / a piece of research
a piece of furniture / an item of furniture
3.2 The three articles and the zero article
There are three articles (a, an, the) and a fourth option, no article at all, called the zero article. Every singular countable noun needs one of these four decided on purpose.

Use a / an for one, non-specific, singular, countable thing, usually mentioned for the first time. The choice between a and an depends on sound, not spelling. Use an before a vowel sound, a before a consonant sound.
a university, a European country (these begin with a “y” consonant sound)
an hour, an honest man (silent h, so a vowel sound)
an MBA, an X-ray (letter names beginning with a vowel sound)
I saw a documentary last night. (first mention, non-specific) / She wants to become an engineer. (one, non-specific)
Use the when the noun is specific: the reader or listener knows exactly which one you mean. That happens in several ways:
It was already mentioned: I saw a documentary. The documentary was about climate change.
There is only one of it: the sun, the government, the internet, the environment.
It is made specific by the words around it: the number of cars, the graph above, the capital of Bangladesh.
With superlatives and ordinals: the highest figure, the most important factor, the first step.
The chart shows the number of visitors. (both specific) / Solar power is the cleanest option available. (superlative)
Plural countable nouns talked about in general: Books are expensive. Cars cause pollution.
Uncountable nouns talked about in general: Water is essential. Education matters. Poverty is rising.
Most proper nouns: names of most countries, cities, people, languages: Bangladesh, Dhaka, English.
Education is a basic right. (general uncountable, zero article) / Cars contribute to pollution. (general plural + general uncountable)
3.3 The decision process (use this when you proofread)
When you check any singular noun, run these questions in order:
Is it countable? If no (uncountable), you cannot use a / an. Choose the (if specific) or zero article (if general). Stop.
If yes (countable): is it specific, known, or unique? If yes, use the.
If it is not specific and singular: use a / an (by sound).
If it is a general plural: use the zero article.
Some article choices are just fixed and should be learned as items:
the internet, the environment, the economy, the government, the media, the public, the world take the (treated as unique).
Superlatives always take the: the best, the largest, the most significant.
Institutions used for their purpose take zero article: go to school, go to university, go to hospital (British usage), in prison, at home. Add the only when you mean the specific building.
Countries: most take zero article (Bangladesh, France, China), but a few plural or “united/republic” names take the: the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, the Philippines.
First mention then second mention: introduce with a, refer back with the. This is the classic a to the move examiners look for: The chart shows a sharp rise in 2018. The rise continued into 2019.
Because Bangla has no articles at all, the category does not exist in your mental grammar, so it must be learned as an English-only system rather than translated. Three error patterns dominate.

Error type 1 · Omitting “the” for specific and unique things.
✗ Internet has changed our lives. / Government should fund school.
✓ The internet has changed our lives. / The government should fund schools.

Error type 2 · Using “a / an” with uncountable nouns. This is the “an advice / an information” error.
✗ He gave me an advice. / She did a research on it.
✓ He gave me some advice / a piece of advice. / She did research / a study on it.

Error type 3 · Dropping the article entirely before a singular countable noun.
✗ Government should take step to reduce pollution.
✓ The government should take steps to reduce pollution.

Article control is audited densely across every task. In Task 1 a single sentence can require three separate article decisions: “The chart shows the number of visitors to a museum.” In Task 2 generalisations, the pattern flips to zero article and the: “Governments should protect the environment.” Because the errors are so frequent, they are the classic thing separating a script that reads like Band 7 in ideas but scores Band 6 in Grammatical Range and Accuracy.

Skills: Writing, Speaking
Task 1: The graph illustrates the proportion of households with an internet connection.
Task 2: Education is widely seen as the key to development, and governments should therefore fund schools properly.
Speaking Part 2: The person who influenced me most was a teacher at my primary school.
End of Chapter 3. Chapter 4 (Prepositions & Dependency Rules) follows.

chapters.title: 3. Practice · Articles (A, An, The) & Noun Types
chapters.group: Module 1 · The Foundational Zero-to-Hero Grammar Engine
blocks: Every singular countable noun needs a deliberate choice: a/an, the, or no article at all. The rule turns on one question -- is this noun specific to both writer and reader, or not?
**Why it matters:** Article errors are some of the most frequent -- and most visible -- mistakes in Bangladeshi candidates' writing, because Bangla has no article system at all.
**a/an** -- one, non-specific, singular, countable thing, usually the first mention. Choice depends on **sound, not spelling**: a university (consonant sound), an hour (silent h, vowel sound).
**the** -- the noun is specific: already mentioned, unique (the sun, the government), or made specific by the words around it (the number of cars).
**zero article** -- plurals and uncountables used in a general sense, and most proper nouns.
Ask: has this been mentioned before, or is there only one of it? If yes, use the. If it's one, unspecified example, use a/an. If neither applies, use no article at all.

blocks.title: Exercise 3.1 · Article Insertion
blocks.instructions: The articles have been removed. Rewrite each sentence inserting a, an, or the where needed. Some blanks need the zero article (no word).

items.prompt: ___ education is ___ key to ___ economic development.
items.answer: Education is the key to economic development.
accepted: Education is the key to economic development.
items.reason: General uncountable “education” and “development” take zero article; “the key” is specific.

items.prompt: She is ___ most hard-working student in ___ class.
items.answer: She is the most hard-working student in the class.
accepted: She is the most hard-working student in the class.
items.reason: Superlative and a specific class both take “the.”

items.prompt: ___ chart shows ___ number of tourists visiting ___ museum.
items.answer: The chart shows the number of tourists visiting a museum.
accepted: The chart shows the number of tourists visiting a museum.
items.reason: “the chart,” “the number of,” first-mention “a museum.”

items.prompt: ___ internet has transformed ___ way people communicate.
items.answer: The internet has transformed the way people communicate.
accepted: The internet has transformed the way people communicate.
items.reason: “the internet” is unique; “the way” is specified by the clause after it.

items.prompt: He wants to become ___ honest lawyer after ___ university.
items.answer: He wants to become an honest lawyer after university.
accepted: He wants to become an honest lawyer after university.
items.reason: “an” before the vowel sound of “honest” (silent h); “university” as an institution takes zero article.

items.prompt: ___ pollution is ___ serious problem in ___ major cities.
items.answer: Pollution is a serious problem in major cities.
accepted: Pollution is a serious problem in major cities.
items.reason: General uncountable “pollution”; “a problem” first mention; general plural “cities.”

items.prompt: I read ___ interesting article yesterday. ___ article was about ___ climate change.
items.answer: I read an interesting article yesterday. The article was about climate change.
accepted: I read an interesting article yesterday. The article was about climate change.
items.reason: First mention “an,” second mention “the,” general “climate change.”

items.prompt: ___ government should invest more in ___ public transport.
items.answer: The government should invest more in public transport.
accepted: The government should invest more in public transport.
items.reason: “the government” is specific; “public transport” is a general uncountable.

items.prompt: ___ United States and ___ United Kingdom signed ___ agreement.
items.answer: The United States and the United Kingdom signed an agreement.
accepted: The United States and the United Kingdom signed an agreement.
items.reason: These country names take “the”; “an agreement” first mention.

items.prompt: ___ sun rises in ___ east.
items.answer: The sun rises in the east.
accepted: The sun rises in the east.
items.reason: Both unique.

items.prompt: ___ poverty remains ___ obstacle to ___ progress in ___ developing world.
items.answer: Poverty remains an obstacle to progress in the developing world.
accepted: Poverty remains an obstacle to progress in the developing world.
items.reason: General “poverty” and “progress”; “an obstacle” first mention; “the developing world” is specific.

items.prompt: She gave me ___ useful advice about ___ visa process.
items.answer: She gave me useful advice about the visa process.
accepted: She gave me useful advice about the visa process.
items.reason: “advice” is uncountable (no “a”); “the visa process” is specific.

items.prompt: ___ number of ___ students who fail ___ exam is rising.
items.answer: The number of students who fail the exam is rising.
accepted: The number of students who fail the exam is rising.
items.reason: “the number of,” general “students,” the specific “exam.”

items.prompt: My brother is ___ engineer, and he works for ___ large company.
items.answer: My brother is an engineer, and he works for a large company.
accepted: My brother is an engineer, and he works for a large company.
items.reason: “an engineer” (vowel sound), “a company” first mention.

items.prompt: ___ water is essential for ___ life on ___ Earth.
items.answer: Water is essential for life on Earth.
accepted: Water is essential for life on Earth.
items.reason: General uncountables and the proper noun “Earth” take zero article.

items.prompt: We stayed in ___ hotel near ___ airport; ___ hotel was cheap.
items.answer: We stayed in a hotel near the airport; the hotel was cheap.
accepted: We stayed in a hotel near the airport; the hotel was cheap.
items.reason: First mention “a hotel,” the known “the airport,” second mention “the hotel.”

items.prompt: ___ research shows that ___ exercise improves ___ mental health.
items.answer: Research shows that exercise improves mental health.
accepted: Research shows that exercise improves mental health.
items.reason: All general/uncountable, zero article.

items.prompt: ___ environment must be protected for ___ future generations.
items.answer: The environment must be protected for future generations.
accepted: The environment must be protected for future generations.
items.reason: “the environment” is unique; “future generations” general plural.

items.prompt: He spent ___ hour reading ___ book about ___ history of ___ Bangladesh.
items.answer: He spent an hour reading a book about the history of Bangladesh.
accepted: He spent an hour reading a book about the history of Bangladesh.
items.reason: “an hour” (silent h), “a book” first mention, “the history of X” specific, proper noun “Bangladesh” zero.

items.prompt: ___ traffic in ___ capital is ___ major source of ___ air pollution.
items.answer: The traffic in the capital is a major source of air pollution.
accepted: The traffic in the capital is a major source of air pollution.
items.reason: “the traffic” specific, “the capital” specific, “a source” first mention, general “air pollution.”

items.prompt: ___ knowledge is power, but ___ information alone is not ___ knowledge.
items.answer: Knowledge is power, but information alone is not knowledge.
accepted: Knowledge is power, but information alone is not knowledge.
items.reason: All general uncountables.

items.prompt: She is ___ best doctor in ___ hospital where I work.
items.answer: She is the best doctor in the hospital where I work.
accepted: She is the best doctor in the hospital where I work.
items.reason: Superlative and a specified hospital.

items.prompt: ___ children in ___ rural areas often lack access to ___ good schools.
items.answer: Children in rural areas often lack access to good schools.
accepted: Children in rural areas often lack access to good schools.
items.reason: General plurals throughout.

items.prompt: ___ economy grew by ___ five per cent in ___ first quarter.
items.answer: The economy grew by five per cent in the first quarter.
accepted: The economy grew by five per cent in the first quarter.
items.reason: “the economy” unique, “five per cent” no article, “the first quarter” ordinal.

items.prompt: ___ solar power is ___ cleaner alternative to ___ fossil fuels.
items.answer: Solar power is a cleaner alternative to fossil fuels.
accepted: Solar power is a cleaner alternative to fossil fuels.
items.reason: General uncountable “solar power,” “a cleaner alternative” first mention, general plural “fossil fuels.”

blocks: Whether a/an is even an option depends on one distinction first: can this noun be counted? Uncountable nouns like information and advice never take a plural -s and never take a/an on their own.
**Why it matters:** This distinction decides whether article and plural rules even apply, so it has to come before everything else in Chapter 3.
**Countable nouns** can be counted and have a plural form: one book, two books. They take a/an in the singular.
**Uncountable nouns** are a single mass, with **no plural form** and **no a/an**: information (never informations), water, advice.
The high-frequency IELTS set to memorise
information, advice, knowledge, research, equipment, furniture, accommodation, traffic, progress, news, money, work, luggage, software, staff, homework.
Use a **partitive phrase**: not an advice but a piece of advice; not a furniture but a piece of furniture or an item of furniture.

blocks.title: Exercise 3.2 · Countable versus Uncountable Error Spotting
blocks.instructions: Each sentence misuses a noun, usually by giving an uncountable noun a plural -s or an a / an. Rewrite each sentence correctly.

items.prompt: The teacher gave us many useful advices before the exam.
items.answer: The teacher gave us much useful advice before the exam.
accepted: The teacher gave us much useful advice before the exam.
items.reason: “advice” is uncountable: no plural, use “much” not “many.”

items.prompt: I need some informations about the application process.
items.answer: I need some information about the application process.
accepted: I need some information about the application process.
items.reason: “information” is uncountable.

items.prompt: She bought new furnitures for her apartment.
items.answer: She bought new furniture for her apartment.
accepted: She bought new furniture for her apartment.
items.reason: “furniture” has no plural; use “pieces of furniture” if counting.

items.prompt: The laboratory does not have enough equipments.
items.answer: The laboratory does not have enough equipment.
accepted: The laboratory does not have enough equipment.
items.reason: “equipment” is uncountable.

items.prompt: He has made a good progress in his studies this year.
items.answer: He has made good progress in his studies this year.
accepted: He has made good progress in his studies this year.
items.reason: “progress” is uncountable: no “a.”

items.prompt: The researchers published several important researches last year.
items.answer: The researchers published several important studies last year.
accepted: The researchers published several important studies last year.
items.reason: “research” is uncountable; the countable word is “studies.”

items.prompt: We had a lot of homeworks during the holidays.
items.answer: We had a lot of homework during the holidays.
accepted: We had a lot of homework during the holidays.
items.reason: “homework” is uncountable.

items.prompt: The company installed new softwares on every computer.
items.answer: The company installed new software on every computer.
accepted: The company installed new software on every computer.
items.reason: “software” is uncountable.

items.prompt: There were many traffics on the road this morning.
items.answer: There was heavy traffic on the road this morning.
accepted: There was heavy traffic on the road this morning.
items.reason: “traffic” is uncountable: no plural, and “was,” not “were.”

items.prompt: The hotel provides free accommodations for its staffs.
items.answer: The hotel provides free accommodation for its staff.
accepted: The hotel provides free accommodation for its staff.
items.reason: both uncountable: no plural.

items.prompt: My knowledges of physics are quite limited.
items.answer: My knowledge of physics is quite limited.
accepted: My knowledge of physics is quite limited.
items.reason: “knowledge” is uncountable and singular.

items.prompt: The government spent a huge money on the project.
items.answer: The government spent a huge amount of money on the project.
accepted: The government spent a huge amount of money on the project.
items.reason: “money” is uncountable: no “a” directly.

items.prompt: She gave me two good news yesterday.
items.answer: She gave me some good news yesterday.
accepted: She gave me some good news yesterday.
She gave me two pieces of good news yesterday.
items.reason: “news” is uncountable despite the final -s.

items.prompt: The students carried heavy luggages to the airport.
items.answer: The students carried heavy luggage to the airport.
accepted: The students carried heavy luggage to the airport.
items.reason: “luggage” is uncountable; count with “pieces of luggage.”

items.prompt: The report contains many useful datas about the economy.
items.answer: The report contains much useful data about the economy.
accepted: The report contains much useful data about the economy.
items.reason: “data” is treated as uncountable/mass here; “datas” is never correct.

chapters.title: 4. Prepositions & Dependency Rules
chapters.group: Module 1 · The Foundational Zero-to-Hero Grammar Engine
blocks: Prepositions of time, place, and direction, the Task 1 data prepositions, dependent prepositions to memorise in blocks, and the direct-translation errors that mark a script as Bangladeshi.

Prepositions are the small words (in, on, at, by, for, to, of, from, with) that show how other words relate in time, place, and direction. They look trivial, but they carry a large share of the errors on this test, for one reason: prepositions are memorised by pattern, not by logic. There is no rule that explains why English says interested in but good at and afraid of. These are fixed collocations, and they either sound right to a native ear or they do not. For a Bangla speaker, that is a problem, because your instinct is to translate the Bangla preposition directly, and Bangla maps its relationships differently.

A preposition sits before a noun or pronoun and shows a relationship: the book is on the table (place), the meeting is at three (time), she walked into the room (direction). The noun after it is called its object. One key rule you already met in the tenses chapter returns here: after a preposition, a verb always takes the -ing form, never the infinitive. Interested in studying, responsible for managing, capable of solving.
4.2 Prepositions of time · in, on, at, and their neighbours
The three core time prepositions follow a “zooming in” logic, from long periods to exact points.
months, years, seasons, centuries, long periods
in July, in 2020, in winter, in the 1990s
on Monday, on 5 May, on weekdays
at 5 p.m., at night, at the weekend, at the start
Other time prepositions that matter for IELTS:
since + a starting point (goes with the present perfect): since 2010, since January.
for + a length of time: for five years, for a decade.
during + a period (when something happens within it): during the 1990s, during the recession.
by + a deadline (not later than): by 2030, by the end of the decade.
from … to / until + a span: from 2000 to 2010, until 2015.
In Monday the shop is closed. / The population grew since five years.
On Monday the shop is closed. / The population grew for five years.
in = inside a space or area: in the room, in Dhaka, in the world.
on = on a surface or line: on the wall, on the coast, on the second floor.
at = at a specific point or place: at the station, at the top, at home.
into / onto / to show movement or direction: walk into the room, climb onto the roof, go to work.
The figures are shown in the chart, on the vertical axis, at the top of the page.
4.4 The Task 1 data prepositions (memorise as fixed phrases)
These combinations describe movement and quantity on a graph. They are non-negotiable in Writing Task 1, and examiners expect every one of them to be exact.
a range or a time span
Sales increased with 20 per cent and reached to a peak in June.
Sales increased by 20 per cent and reached a peak in June.
“increase by” a percentage; “reach a peak” takes no preposition after “reach.”
A single strong Task 1 sentence often chains several of these: The price rose by five dollars, from 20 to 25, reaching a peak of 25 in March.
4.5 Dependent prepositions (the ones after specific words)
Many verbs, adjectives, and nouns are followed by a fixed preposition. There is no logic; you learn each as a unit. Memorise them in blocks and use them until they feel automatic.
The policy resulted in higher costs.
The panel consists of five experts.
The essay focuses on two causes.
Families struggle to cope with rising costs.
Individuals are responsible for their choices.
People are more aware of the risks.
The system is capable of handling demand.
This trend is similar to the previous one.
Urban life is different from rural life.
He is good at solving problems.
The economy is dependent on exports.
The issue is related to poverty.
The course is suitable for beginners.

These are the specific errors that come from translating a Bangla structure word for word. They are extremely common and instantly recognisable to an examiner, so fixing them gives a fast, visible accuracy gain.

discuss / enter / reach / marry take a direct object - no preposition
✗ discuss about the topic / enter into the room / reach to the destination / marry with her
✓ discuss the topic / enter the room / reach the destination / marry her

according to me / return back / comprise of / mention about / cope up with
✗ According to me / return back home / comprise of three parts / mention about it / cope up with
✓ In my opinion / return home / comprise three parts / mention it / cope with

Prepositions affect your score in two visible places. In Writing Task 1, the data prepositions (by, from, to, of, at) are so standard that getting one wrong stands out immediately as an accuracy error. In Writing Task 2 and Speaking, the dependent prepositions (depend on, lead to, responsible for, solution to) and the direct-translation errors (discuss about, according to me) separate controlled from uncontrolled English. Because these are collocations, correct ones also lift your Lexical Resource score, so the payoff is double.

Skills: Writing, Speaking
Task 1: Unemployment rose by four points, from six to ten per cent, before falling to eight in 2015.
Task 2: A lack of investment in public transport contributes to congestion and leads to higher emissions.
Speaking Part 3: It really depends on the situation, but on balance I think education is the solution to most of these problems.
End of Chapter 4, and of Module 1. Module 2 (Band 7.0+ Complex Structures), Chapter 5 follows.

chapters.title: 4. Practice · Prepositions & Dependency Rules
chapters.group: Module 1 · The Foundational Zero-to-Hero Grammar Engine
blocks: Many verbs, adjectives, and nouns are locked to a specific preposition with no logic behind the pairing -- you simply have to memorise each one as a fixed unit: depend ON, responsible FOR, an increase IN.
**Why it matters:** Dependent prepositions are pure memorisation, but they're everywhere in academic writing, and getting them wrong reads as a basic error even in an otherwise strong sentence.
Learn them in blocks, by word type
**Verb + preposition:** depend on, lead to, result in, result from.
**Adjective + preposition:** responsible for, interested in, aware of, capable of.
**Noun + preposition:** an increase/rise in, a reason for, a solution to, an effect/impact on.
There's no shortcut here -- memorise each pairing as a single chunk, not as two separate words, and practise them inside full sentences until the pairing feels automatic rather than looked-up.

blocks.title: Exercise 4.1 · Preposition Fill-in
blocks.instructions: Fill each gap with the correct preposition. Some gaps take no preposition; write (0) for those.

items.prompt: The number of tourists rose ______ 20 per cent last year.
items.answer: by
accepted: by
items.reason: The size of a change.

items.prompt: The figure grew ______ 5 million ______ 8 million ______ 2015.
items.answer: from / to / in
accepted: from / to / in
from to in
from, to, in
items.reason: Start, end, and the year.

blocks: A preposition shows a relationship -- place, time, or direction -- and its object follows it. When your English feels subtly wrong, check whether you've translated a Bangla preposition pattern directly instead of using the fixed English one.
**Why it matters:** Most preposition errors from Bangla speakers come from translating the L1 pattern word-for-word rather than learning the English pairing as its own fixed unit.
A preposition sits before a noun or pronoun and shows a relationship: on the table (place), at three (time), into the room (direction). The noun that follows is called its object.

Whenever a preposition feels uncertain, resist translating from Bangla directly. Instead, recall the fixed English phrase as a whole chunk -- depend on, not "depend from" or "depend of" -- since English prepositions rarely map one-to-one onto their Bangla equivalents.

chapters.title: 5. Complex Sentences & Subordinate Clauses
chapters.group: Module 2 · Band 7.0+ Complex Structures & Range Booster
blocks: The single most important structure for Band 7. Clause basics, the three sentence types, adverbial and relative clauses, the comma rule, and fixing fragments, run-ons, and comma splices.

Module 1 made your sentences correct. Module 2 makes them varied. This is the stage where scripts stop sounding like a list of short, safe statements and start reading like connected argument. The Band 7 descriptor for Grammatical Range and Accuracy asks for “a variety of complex structures used with some flexibility,” and this module supplies exactly that: complex sentences built from subordinate clauses, the passive voice for academic tone, and conditionals for arguing about possibilities.

The complex sentence is the single most important structure for reaching Band 7, because it is the clearest signal of range. It lets you show a logical relationship between two ideas (contrast, reason, condition, time) inside one controlled sentence, instead of two short disconnected ones.
A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb. There are two kinds, and the whole chapter rests on telling them apart.
An independent clause expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence: “Cities offer jobs.”

A dependent (subordinate) clause has a subject and a verb but cannot stand alone, because a subordinating word at its front leaves it unfinished: “Although cities offer jobs …” This makes you wait for the rest.
A complex sentence joins one independent clause with at least one dependent clause: Although cities offer jobs, (dependent) they are crowded. (independent)
5.2 The three sentence types, and why complex wins marks
Cities offer jobs, but they are crowded.
Although cities offer jobs, they are crowded.

A Band 5 script is mostly simple sentences. A Band 6 script mixes simple and compound. A Band 7 script controls complex sentences and uses a variety of them. There are two main tools: adverbial clauses (5.3) and relative clauses (5.4).

An adverbial clause is a dependent clause that begins with a subordinating conjunction and shows how its idea relates to the main clause. Learn the subordinators grouped by the relationship they signal.
Although it is costly, it works.
Prices rose because demand outstripped supply.
if, unless, provided that, as long as
Unless action is taken, the trend will continue.
Laws were tightened so that accidents would fall.
The cost was so high that the plan collapsed.
For purpose, the most useful compact form is in order to + base verb (or simply to + base verb): The city expanded the metro in order to reduce congestion.

If the dependent clause comes first, put a comma after it. If it comes second, usually use no comma. Although it is costly, it works. (fronted dependent clause, comma) / It works although it is costly. (dependent clause second, no comma)

A relative clause adds information about a noun using a relative pronoun: who, which, that, where, whose. It lets you fold what would be two short sentences into one mature sentence, which directly serves range.
Students who study abroad gain independence.
Solar power, which is clean, is expanding.
The policy that failed was expensive.
Cities where rents are high lose young workers.
Families whose income is low need support.
Defining versus non-defining: the comma changes the meaning
This is the part that carries the marks, and it is not decorative. The commas change what the sentence means.
A defining clause identifies which one and is essential. It takes no commas. Students who cheat are expelled. (only the cheating ones)
A non-defining clause adds extra, non-essential information and is fenced with commas on both sides. The students, who were tired, left early. (all of them)
Use that only in defining clauses. In non-defining clauses use which or who, never that. Wrong: My school, that is very old, is famous. Right: My school, which is very old, is famous.

Do not repeat the subject with a pronoun after the relative clause. This is a very common Bangladeshi error. Wrong: People which live in cities they pay more rent. Right: People who live in cities pay more rent.

Reduced relative clauses (a Band 8 touch): You can often drop the relative pronoun and the verb be to make a tighter phrase. Governments that invest in renewables … → Governments investing in renewables … / The report which was published last year … → The report published last year …

When learners first attempt complex sentences, three punctuation faults appear. All three come from not yet feeling where one clause ends and the next begins. The four legal ways to join two independent clauses: a full stop, a semicolon, a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS), or by turning one clause into a dependent clause with a subordinator. A lone comma is never one of them.

Fault 1 · The fragment (a dependent clause left alone).
✗ Because the weather was bad. The event was cancelled.
✓ Because the weather was bad, the event was cancelled.

Fault 2 · The run-on (two clauses with no join).
✗ I studied hard I failed the exam.
✓ I studied hard, but I failed the exam.

Fault 3 · The comma splice (two clauses joined by only a comma).
✗ Internet use rose rapidly, people spent more time online.
✓ Internet use rose rapidly, so people spent more time online.

The phrase in the official Band 7 descriptor is “a variety of complex structures.” That word variety matters: an essay that uses only because clauses does not show range, even if every one is correct. Aim to deploy a spread across a Task 2 essay: a contrast clause (although), a reason clause (since), a conditional (if), and a relative clause or two.

Skills: Writing, Speaking
Task 2 (contrast + relative): While online learning widens access, it cannot fully replace the discipline that a classroom provides.
Task 2 (reason + condition): Because demand continues to rise, prices will keep climbing unless supply increases.
Speaking Part 3: People who grow up in cities often value convenience, whereas those from rural areas tend to prioritise community.
End of Chapter 5. Chapter 6 (Passive Voice & Academic Detachment) follows.

chapters.title: 5. Practice · Complex Sentences & Subordinate Clauses
chapters.group: Module 2 · Band 7.0+ Complex Structures & Range Booster
blocks: Simple sentences get you to Band 5. Complex sentences -- one independent clause plus a dependent clause -- are what a Band 7 script controls and varies. Learn the two main tools: adverbial clauses and relative clauses.
**Why it matters:** Sentence variety is graded directly, and complex sentences are the single biggest lever for moving from Band 5-6 writing into Band 7+.
Cities offer jobs, but they are crowded.
Although cities offer jobs, they are crowded.

A Band 5 script is mostly simple sentences. A Band 6 script mixes simple and compound. A **Band 7 script controls complex sentences and varies them** -- using both adverbial clauses (if/although/because) and relative clauses (who/which/that).

blocks.title: Exercise 5.1 · Sentence Combining
blocks.instructions: Combine each pair of simple sentences into one complex sentence, using the relationship in brackets and either a relative clause or an adverbial clause.

accepted: Although public transport is cheap, many people still drive.

accepted: Although renewable energy is expensive at first, it becomes cheaper over time.

accepted: The report, which was published last year, highlighted the housing crisis.
items.reason: Non-defining relative clause: commas.

accepted: Unless action is taken soon, the situation will worsen.

items.answer: Many families who live in rural areas lack access to good hospitals.
accepted: Many families who live in rural areas lack access to good hospitals.
items.reason: Defining relative clause.

items.answer: Although the policy was popular, it was eventually withdrawn.
accepted: Although the policy was popular, it was eventually withdrawn.
items.reason: Contrast clause.

items.prompt: Solar power is clean. It is expanding rapidly. (relative, non-defining)
items.answer: Solar power, which is clean, is expanding rapidly.
accepted: Solar power, which is clean, is expanding rapidly.
items.reason: Non-defining relative clause: commas.

items.prompt: Demand outstripped supply. Prices rose sharply. (reason)
items.answer: Prices rose sharply because demand outstripped supply.
accepted: Prices rose sharply because demand outstripped supply.
items.reason: Reason clause.

items.prompt: Students study abroad. They gain independence and confidence. (relative)
items.answer: Students who study abroad gain independence and confidence.
accepted: Students who study abroad gain independence and confidence.
items.reason: Defining relative clause.

items.prompt: The factory closed in 1998. Hundreds of workers lost their jobs. (time / result)
items.answer: When the factory closed in 1998, hundreds of workers lost their jobs.
accepted: When the factory closed in 1998, hundreds of workers lost their jobs.
items.reason: Time clause.

items.prompt: Cities are crowded and expensive. Young workers often leave them. (reason)
items.answer: Because cities are crowded and expensive, young workers often leave them.
accepted: Because cities are crowded and expensive, young workers often leave them.
items.reason: Reason clause.

items.prompt: The government raises taxes. Public services can be funded properly. (purpose)
items.answer: The government raises taxes so that public services can be funded properly.
accepted: The government raises taxes so that public services can be funded properly.
items.reason: Purpose clause.

items.prompt: This is the town. I grew up there. (relative, place)
items.answer: This is the town where I grew up.
accepted: This is the town where I grew up.
items.reason: Relative clause of place with “where.”

items.prompt: Technology keeps advancing. Many traditional jobs are disappearing. (concession)
items.answer: Even though technology keeps advancing, many traditional jobs are disappearing.
accepted: Even though technology keeps advancing, many traditional jobs are disappearing.
items.reason: Concession clause.

items.prompt: Some countries recycle most of their waste. Others send it to landfill. (contrast)
items.answer: While some countries recycle most of their waste, others send it to landfill.
accepted: While some countries recycle most of their waste, others send it to landfill.
items.reason: Contrast clause with “while.”

blocks: Defining and non-defining relative clauses look almost identical -- the only difference is a pair of commas, but that punctuation changes the meaning of the sentence entirely.
**Why it matters:** This is the part of relative clauses that actually carries marks -- the commas aren't decorative, they change what the sentence means.
A **defining clause** identifies which one and is essential -- no commas: Students who cheat are expelled (only the cheating ones).
A **non-defining clause** adds extra, non-essential information, fenced with commas on both sides: The students, who were tired, left early (all of them).
Use **that** only in defining clauses. In non-defining clauses, use **which** or **who** -- never that.
Don't repeat the subject with a pronoun after the relative clause (a very common Bangla-influenced error).
Reduced relative clauses tighten the sentence further: governments that invest in renewables → governments investing in renewables.

blocks.title: Exercise 5.2 · Punctuation and Relative-Clause Polish

accepted: Students who cheat in exams are usually expelled.

accepted: The report was clear; it recommended three changes.

items.answer: Although the policy was expensive, it reduced accidents significantly.
accepted: Although the policy was expensive, it reduced accidents significantly.

accepted: Solar power, which is renewable, is becoming cheaper.

accepted: People who live near factories often suffer from poor air quality.

items.answer: Governments that invest in transport tend to see lower long-term costs.
accepted: Governments that invest in transport tend to see lower long-term costs.

items.answer: Correct.
accepted: Correct.
Correct

items.answer: Because the weather was extremely bad, the outdoor event was postponed.

chapters.title: 6. Passive Voice & Academic Detachment
chapters.group: Module 2 · Band 7.0+ Complex Structures & Range Booster
blocks: The passive across every tense you need, when to choose it, the impersonal “It is …” frames for academic detachment, and the twin pitfalls: wrong participles and overuse.

The passive voice turns the object of an action into the subject of the sentence, so the focus falls on what happens rather than who does it. It is one of the two or three structures that give academic writing its formal, impersonal tone, and it is essential in two specific IELTS places: the Task 1 process diagram, which is written almost entirely in the passive, and the Task 2 essay, where an impersonal register sounds more objective than a personal one. Used well, the passive lifts your tone; used everywhere, it makes writing heavy and evasive.

Compare two sentences that describe the same event: Active: Workers transport the materials. (subject = workers, the doer) / Passive: The materials are transported (by workers). (subject = materials, the receiver)

In the active voice, the subject does the action. In the passive voice, the subject receives the action, and the doer either disappears or is added at the end with by. The formula never changes: Object of the active sentence + a form of be + past participle (+ by + doer). Get the correct form of be (which carries the tense) and the past participle right and the passive is right.
The tense lives in the be part; the past participle stays the same. This table shows the transformation for the tenses you actually need.
Notice the pattern: whatever the tense, you always end with the past participle (transported), and the be form in front of it changes to carry the time.
The passive is a tool for specific situations, not a default. Use it when:
The doer is unknown, obvious, or unimportant. New traffic laws were introduced in 2019. (who introduced them is obvious).
You want an objective, impersonal tone. It is widely believed that education reduces poverty. (more academic than “Many people believe …”)
You are describing a process. First, the raw beans are harvested. They are then dried, roasted, and ground before the coffee is packaged.
6.4 Academic detachment: the impersonal “It is …” structures
A specific, high-value use of the passive is to remove “I” and “people” from a general claim, which sounds more objective. Learn these frames:
People say that tourism harms the coast.
It is said that tourism harms the coast.
Get the past participle right, and do not overuse

The passive needs the third form of the verb, not the base form or the past simple. Bangladeshi learners often drop the participle ending. Irregular past participles must be memorised (see Appendix A): build/built, write/written, take/taken, give/given, show/shown. Also, do not overuse the passive: a whole essay in the passive reads as stiff and can hide who is responsible. In Task 2, mix passive and active.

Pitfall 1 · A missing or wrong past participle.
✗ The materials are transport to the site. / The bridge was build in 1990. / The report was wrote by the committee.
✓ The materials are transported to the site. / The bridge was built in 1990. / The report was written by the committee.

Pitfall 2 · Overusing the passive. The passive belongs mainly in the Task 1 process and in impersonal general claims; your arguments and opinions are usually clearer in the active.
✗ (whole essay in the passive)
✓ (mix passive and active; arguments in the active)

Writing Task 1 process diagrams are the clearest case: because the doer of each step is irrelevant, the whole description runs in the passive present simple. A process answer that stays in the active sounds childish; the passive is expected. Writing Task 2 uses the passive more selectively, for the impersonal tone of general statements. Combined with the active for your own arguments, it shows the examiner you can control register.

Skills: Writing, Speaking
Task 1 process: Once the cocoa pods have been harvested, the beans are removed, fermented, and left to dry in the sun.
Task 2 impersonal: It is often argued that stricter regulation is needed, although the costs are frequently underestimated.
Speaking Part 3: A lot is being done to improve recycling, but more could be achieved with better public awareness.
End of Chapter 6. Chapter 7 (Conditionals, Hedging & Hypothetical Reasoning) follows.

chapters.title: 6. Practice · Passive Voice & Academic Detachment
chapters.group: Module 2 · Band 7.0+ Complex Structures & Range Booster
blocks: Whatever the tense, the passive always ends in the past participle -- only the 'be' form in front of it changes to carry the time. Learn that one pattern and you can transform any active sentence.
**Why it matters:** The passive appears across every tense, and IELTS Task 1 and academic writing lean on it constantly -- so the transformation needs to be automatic.
The tense lives in the **be** part; the past participle stays the same.
Present simple: Workers transport the goods. → The goods are transported.
Present continuous: Workers are transporting the goods. → The goods are being transported.
Past simple: Workers transported the goods. → The goods were transported.
Notice the constant: whatever the tense, you always end with the past participle (transported), and only the be form in front of it changes to carry the time.

blocks.title: Exercise 6.1 · Active to Passive Transformation
blocks.instructions: Rewrite each active sentence in the passive voice, keeping the same tense. Drop the doer where it is obvious, or keep it with “by” where it adds meaning.

items.prompt: Farmers harvest the crop in October.
items.answer: The crop is harvested in October.
accepted: The crop is harvested in October.
The crop is harvested by farmers in October.
items.reason: present simple.

items.prompt: The council will build a new bridge next year.
items.answer: A new bridge will be built next year.
accepted: A new bridge will be built next year.
items.reason: future.

items.prompt: The committee wrote the report.
items.answer: The report was written by the committee.
accepted: The report was written by the committee.

blocks: Recap · Passive Voice for Process Writing

The passive isn't a default -- it's a tool for three specific situations: when the doer is unknown or obvious, when you want an objective tone, and when you're describing a process. Process diagrams are exactly that third case.
**Why it matters:** Process-diagram Task 1s are almost impossible to write naturally without the passive, since the steps matter more than who performs them.
The **doer is unknown, obvious, or unimportant**: New traffic laws were introduced in 2019 (who introduced them is obvious).
You want an **objective, impersonal tone**: It is widely believed that education reduces poverty (more academic than "many people believe").
You are **describing a process** -- a sequence of steps where the focus is the material or product moving through stages, not the people carrying them out.
For process diagrams specifically, keep every step in the passive and in a consistent tense (usually present simple) so the sequence reads as a system, not a story about workers.

blocks.title: Exercise 6.2 · Process Diagram Writing
blocks.instructions: Write one paragraph of about 150 words using the passive present simple throughout and appropriate sequencing words (first, then, next, after that, once, finally).

items.prompt: Write one paragraph of about 150 words describing how glass bottles are recycled, using the passive present simple throughout and sequencing words. Stages: used glass bottles collected from homes and bins; transported to a recycling plant; sorted by colour; washed to remove labels and dirt; crushed into small pieces called cullet; melted in a furnace at very high temperature; moulded into new bottles; new bottles filled, labelled, and sent to shops.
items.answer: The diagram illustrates the process by which used glass bottles are recycled into new ones. First, used bottles are collected from homes and public bins, after which they are transported to a recycling plant. On arrival, the glass is sorted by colour into clear, green, and brown, and it is then washed thoroughly so that labels and dirt are removed. Next, the clean glass is crushed into small fragments known as cullet. Once this stage is complete, the cullet is melted in a furnace at an extremely high temperature until it becomes liquid. The molten glass is then moulded into the shape of new bottles. Finally, the finished bottles are filled, labelled, and sent to shops, where the cycle can begin again.
accepted: The diagram illustrates the process by which used glass bottles are recycled into new ones. First, used bottles are collected from homes and public bins, after which they are transported to a recycling plant. On arrival, the glass is sorted by colour into clear, green, and brown, and it is then washed thoroughly so that labels and dirt are removed. Next, the clean glass is crushed into small fragments known as cullet. Once this stage is complete, the cullet is melted in a furnace at an extremely high temperature until it becomes liquid. The molten glass is then moulded into the shape of new bottles. Finally, the finished bottles are filled, labelled, and sent to shops, where the cycle can begin again.
items.reason: Every step is in the passive present simple (are collected, is sorted, is melted, are sent) because the doer is irrelevant; the sequence is held together by ordering words (first, then, next, once, finally); the tense stays consistent from start to finish.

chapters.title: 7. Conditionals, Hedging & Hypothetical Reasoning
chapters.group: Module 2 · Band 7.0+ Complex Structures & Range Booster
blocks: The four conditionals as a scale of reality, the first-vs-second choice that matters most in Task 2, the one rule that removes most conditional errors, and the hedging toolkit for academic caution.

Conditionals let you argue about possibilities: what happens if something is true, what would happen if it were, and what would have happened if the past had been different. This is the grammar of consequence and hypothesis, and it is central to Task 2, where almost every argument is really a conditional in disguise: if governments do X, then Y will follow. Alongside conditionals sits hedging, the language of caution (may, tend to, it is likely that), which stops your claims from sounding absolute and makes your writing sound measured and academic.

Every conditional has an if-clause (the condition) and a main clause (the result). The order is free; if the if-clause comes first, it is followed by a comma. If demand rises, prices increase. = Prices increase if demand rises. The four standard conditionals differ only in the tense pattern across those two clauses, and each expresses a different degree of reality.
If you heat ice, it melts.
If taxes rise, consumption will fall.
If I were rich, I would fund schools.
If they had invested, the crisis would have been avoided.

Read the table as a scale of reality: zero is always true, first is realistically possible, second is imagined or unlikely, third is impossible now because the moment has passed. Choosing the right one is choosing how real you want the claim to sound.
A note on “were” in the second conditional: formal English uses were for all subjects (“If the government were to act …”), and this is the safer choice in Writing.
7.3 First versus second: the choice that matters most in Task 2
Most of your conditional errors and choices come down to first versus second, so drill this pair.
Use the first conditional for a real proposal you think is genuinely possible. If the government invests in public transport, congestion will decrease.
Use the second conditional for a hypothetical or a suggestion you are framing as imagined. If every citizen planted a tree, the city would be greener.
If the government will raise taxes, spending falls.
If the government raises taxes, spending will fall.
The if-clause of a first conditional takes the present simple, never “will.”
If I would be in charge, I would ban cars.
If I were in charge, I would ban cars.
The if-clause of a second conditional takes the past simple / “were,” never “would.”
The one rule that removes most conditional errors

Never put “will” or “would” in the if-clause. “Will” and “would” live in the result clause only. Keep the if-clause in a simple/past tense and you eliminate the most common conditional mistake in a single move.
7.4 Mixed and inverted conditionals (a Band 8+ touch)
Two advanced moves add range when they fit naturally:
Mixed conditional: a past condition with a present result. If they had planned better (past), the city would not be so congested now (present).
Inverted conditional (formal, drops “if”): Had the government acted sooner, the crisis would have been avoided. = If the government had acted sooner … (You will meet inversion fully in Chapter 8.)
Use these once, accurately, for effect. A forced mixed conditional is worse than a clean standard one.
7.5 Hedging: the language of academic caution

Hedging means softening a claim so it is not an absolute statement. Band 5 writing is full of overstatements (always, never, everyone, will definitely). Band 8 writing qualifies its claims, which paradoxically makes them sound more credible and more academic. This is one of the fastest ways to raise the maturity of your tone.
tend to, be likely to, appear to, seem to
often, generally, in many cases, to some extent, relatively
it is likely that, it appears that, there is a tendency for
many, some, a significant number of, the majority of
Junk food always causes obesity and will destroy public health.
Excessive consumption of junk food may contribute to obesity and could place a strain on public health.
“always causes” and “will destroy” are overstated; “may contribute” and “could place a strain” are measured.

Hedging is not weakness or vagueness. It is precision about how certain you are. “Immigration boosts the economy” is a claim you cannot fully prove; “Immigration can boost the economy” is one you can defend.

Two clusters of error dominate. The first is tense leakage in conditionals (putting will/would in the if-clause). The second is the habit of writing sweeping absolutes, which comes partly from the strength of assertion common in Bangla essay style.

Error type 1 · “will/would” in the if-clause.
✗ If the price will increase, demand will fall. / If governments would ban plastic, pollution would drop.
✓ If the price increases, demand will fall. / If governments banned plastic, pollution would drop.

Error type 2 · Unqualified absolutes.
✗ Technology always improves our lives. / Every student prefers online classes.
✓ Technology generally improves our lives. / Many students appear to prefer online classes.
Conditionals and hedging together define Task 2 maturity

Task 2 rewards two things this chapter delivers. Conditionals give you the structure to argue consequences (“if this policy is adopted, then …”), which is the backbone of a body paragraph. Hedging gives you the tone to make those arguments sound reasoned rather than dogmatic. A script that combines an accurate second conditional with well-placed hedging reads as clearly Band 7-plus, because it shows both grammatical range and rhetorical control.

Skills: Writing, Speaking
Task 2 (first conditional): If governments subsidise clean energy, the transition away from fossil fuels is likely to accelerate.
Task 2 (second + hedge): If education were entirely free, access might improve, though the burden on public finances would probably be considerable.
Speaking Part 3: It tends to depend on the context, but on the whole I'd say technology has made communication easier.
End of Chapter 7, and of Module 2. Module 3 (Band 9.0 Masterclass), Chapter 8 follows.

chapters.title: 7. Practice · Conditionals, Hedging & Hypothetical Reasoning
chapters.group: Module 2 · Band 7.0+ Complex Structures & Range Booster
blocks: The four conditionals sit on a scale of reality, from always-true to no-longer-possible. Choosing the right one is choosing how real you want your claim to sound -- get this wrong and a genuine possibility reads as pure fantasy, or vice versa.
**Why it matters:** Conditional choice signals how confident you are in a claim, which matters enormously in Task 2 argumentation.
The four conditionals, as a scale of reality
**Zero** -- general truth / scientific fact: If you heat ice, it melts.
**First** -- a real, likely future possibility: If taxes rise, consumption will fall.
**Third** -- impossible now, because the moment has passed.
Read the scale in order: zero is always true, first is realistically possible, second is imagined, third is impossible.
Formal English uses **were** for all subjects in the second conditional -- If the government were to act... -- and this is the safer choice in Writing.

blocks: Band 5 writing is full of absolutes -- always, never, everyone. Band 8 writing hedges its claims with modals and tendency verbs, which paradoxically makes them sound more credible, not less confident.
**Why it matters:** Hedging is one of the fastest, most learnable upgrades from Band 6-7 writing into Band 8 writing -- it's a toolkit, not a talent.
Hedging softens a claim so it isn't an absolute statement. "Immigration boosts the economy" is a claim you can't fully prove; "Immigration can boost the economy" is one you can defend.
**Modal verbs of possibility:** may, might, could, can.
**Verbs of tendency:** tend to, be likely to, appear to, seem to.
**Adverbs of frequency/degree:** often, generally, in many cases, to some extent, relatively.
**Impersonal frames:** it is often argued that, it could be said that.
Hedging is not weakness or vagueness -- it's precision about how certain you actually are.

blocks.title: Exercise 7.2 · Hedging Upgrade Drill
