chapters.title: 8. Inversion, Cleft Sentences & Advanced Emphasis
blocks: The rare, high-band emphasis structures: negative-adverbial inversion built with question word order, it-clefts and what-clefts, and the discipline of using one, accurately, rather than many.

Welcome to the Band 9 masterclass. Everything from here is about precision and sophistication, not correction. The structures in this module are the ones that appear naturally in the writing of highly proficient users: they are rare, they create emphasis, and they must be used sparingly and accurately. One well-placed inversion signals mastery; three forced ones signal a candidate who has memorised a trick. Quality and control, not quantity, is the entire message of Module 3.

Inversion means reversing the normal subject-verb order so that the verb (or auxiliary) comes before the subject, the pattern you normally only see in questions. In statements, we do it deliberately for emphasis, usually by moving a negative or limiting expression to the front of the sentence. When such an expression leads, the subject and auxiliary swap places. Normal: The government has rarely intervened. / Inverted: Rarely has the government intervened.

The mechanism is exactly the question mechanism: front the negative adverbial, then use question word order (auxiliary + subject). If there is no auxiliary, introduce do / does / did, just as in questions. Normal: The minister realised the scale of the problem only later. / Inverted: Only later did the minister realise the scale of the problem.
8.2 The trigger expressions (learn these as a set)
Inversion is triggered when one of these negative or limiting adverbials is moved to the front. Memorise the set; they are the entry ticket.
Never before has the country faced such a crisis.
Rarely do politicians admit their mistakes.
Not only does it cut costs, but it also saves time.
No sooner had the policy begun than it was criticised.
Hardly had the scheme started when problems emerged.
Only after / Only when / Only by
Only by investing heavily can the goal be achieved.
Under no circumstances should this be ignored.
Little did they know how costly it would be.
Not until 2015 did the figures begin to recover.
8.3 How to build an inverted sentence, step by step
Start with the plain sentence: The government has seldom acted so quickly.
Choose the trigger and move it to the front: Seldom …
Apply question word order (auxiliary before subject): Seldom has the government …
Complete the sentence: Seldom has the government acted so quickly.

If the original has no auxiliary, add do / does / did and return the main verb to its base form, exactly as when forming a question. The committee only later understood the risk. → Only later did the committee understand the risk. (not “understood”)

A cleft sentence (from “cleave,” to split) divides one idea into two clauses so as to spotlight one element. It is a gentler, more common emphasis tool than inversion and is very natural in both Writing and Speaking. There are two main patterns.

Structure: It + is/was + the emphasised element + that/who + the rest. Plain: The lack of funding caused the failure. / Cleft: It was the lack of funding that caused the failure. (spotlight on the cause)
Structure: What + clause + is/was + the emphasised element. Plain: We need better public transport. / Cleft: What we need is better public transport. (spotlight on the solution)
The what-cleft is especially useful for opening a point emphatically in an essay or a Speaking answer: What many governments overlook is the long-term cost of inaction.
Do not break agreement or over-deploy
The danger with these structures is not the concept but the execution. Two failures recur.

Failure 1 · Forgetting question word order after the trigger. The subject and auxiliary must swap; keeping normal order cancels the inversion.
✗ Never before the country has faced such a crisis. / Rarely politicians admit their mistakes.
✓ Never before has the country faced such a crisis. / Rarely do politicians admit their mistakes.

Failure 2 · Over-deployment. Using several inversions or clefts in one answer makes writing sound theatrical and unnatural. One accurate example, placed at a genuinely emphatic moment, is the goal.
✗ (three inversions in one paragraph)
✓ (one well-placed inversion, the rest in normal order)
A single inversion can lift a whole script

Inversion and clefts are not everyday grammar; they are the flourishes that mark the top band. Examiners looking to justify Band 8 or 9 in Grammatical Range and Accuracy look for exactly this: evidence that the candidate can produce rare, complex forms accurately and naturally. The strategic use is one inversion or cleft placed at the most important sentence of an essay or a Speaking Part 3 answer, the point you most want to emphasise. Done once, cleanly, it is a strong positive signal. Overused, it works against you.

Skills: Writing, Speaking
Task 2 (inversion): Not only does renewable energy reduce emissions, but it also creates long-term employment.
Task 2 (what-cleft): What is often forgotten in this debate is the cost of doing nothing.
Speaking Part 3 (it-cleft): It was really the support of my family that made the biggest difference.
End of Chapter 8. Chapter 9 (Nominalisation & Academic Density) follows.

chapters.title: 8. Practice · Inversion, Cleft Sentences & Advanced Emphasis
blocks: Inversion fires when a negative or limiting adverbial moves to the front of the sentence -- never, rarely, not only. Learn this trigger set as a fixed list and the auxiliary-before-subject pattern becomes automatic.
**Why it matters:** Correct inversion is one of the clearest Band 9 signals an examiner looks for -- and one of the easiest to get wrong if attempted carelessly.
Inversion is triggered when one of these negative or limiting adverbials moves to the front:
**Never / Never before** -- Never before has the country faced such a crisis.
**Rarely / Seldom** -- Rarely do politicians admit their mistakes.
**Not only... (but also)** -- Not only does it cut costs, but it also saves time.
Memorise the trigger set first. Once the trigger is at the front, the subject and auxiliary verb swap places exactly as they do in a question -- that's the whole mechanism.

blocks.instructions: Rewrite each sentence beginning with the negative or limiting expression, applying question word order. Where a sentence is already inverted incorrectly, fix it.

It-cleft

accepted: Never before had people had access to so much information.

blocks: A cleft sentence splits one idea into two clauses to spotlight a single element. It's gentler than inversion and far more natural in both Writing and Speaking -- two patterns cover almost every use.
**Why it matters:** Cleft sentences are a natural, low-risk way to add emphasis without the stricter grammar rules that inversion demands.
Structure: **It + is/was + the emphasised element + that/who + the rest.**
Plain: The lack of funding caused the failure. → Cleft: It was the lack of funding that caused the failure. (spotlight on the cause)
Structure: **What + clause + is/was + the emphasised element.**
Plain: We need better public transport. → Cleft: What we need is better public transport. (spotlight on the solution)
The what-cleft is especially useful for opening a point emphatically: What many governments overlook is the long-term cost of inaction.

blocks.title: Exercise 8.2 · Cleft Sentence Construction

items.answer: What people overlook is the long-term costs.
accepted: What people overlook is the long-term costs.
items.reason: What-cleft.

items.prompt: Emphasise the person with an it-cleft: My mentor changed my career.
items.answer: It was my mentor who changed my career.
accepted: It was my mentor who changed my career.
items.reason: It-cleft with “who” for a person.

items.prompt: Emphasise the real issue with a what-cleft: The real issue is a lack of funding.
items.answer: What matters most is the lack of funding.
accepted: What matters most is the lack of funding.
What the real issue is is a lack of funding.
What is really at stake is the lack of funding.
items.reason: What-cleft foregrounding the key issue.

items.prompt: Emphasise the place with an it-cleft: The decision was made in Parliament.
items.answer: It was in Parliament that the decision was made.
accepted: It was in Parliament that the decision was made.
items.reason: It-cleft on the place.

items.prompt: Emphasise the action needed with a what-cleft: Governments must act now.
items.answer: What governments must do now is act.
accepted: What governments must do now is act.
What governments need to do now is act.
items.reason: What-cleft on the required action.

items.prompt: Emphasise the factor with an it-cleft: Education drives development.
items.answer: It is education that drives development.
accepted: It is education that drives development.
items.reason: It-cleft on the driver.

items.prompt: Emphasise the priority with a what-cleft: We should prioritise public health.
items.answer: What we should prioritise is public health.
accepted: What we should prioritise is public health.
items.reason: What-cleft on the priority.

chapters.title: 9. Nominalisation & Academic Density
blocks: The verb/adjective-to-noun transformation that defines academic register, three restructuring moves for Task 2, nominalisation as a cohesion device, and the discipline of not over-nominalising into fog.

Nominalisation is the process of turning a verb or an adjective into a noun, and it is the single most characteristic feature of formal academic English. Where everyday speech says “the government decided to act, and this reduced pollution,” academic writing says “the government's decision to act led to a reduction in pollution.” The information is identical; the register is transformed. Nominalisation lets you pack more meaning into fewer words, connect ideas smoothly, and adopt the impersonal, concept-focused tone that examiners associate with the highest bands.

Nominalisation converts an action word (verb) or a quality word (adjective) into a thing word (noun). Once an idea is a noun, it can become the subject of a sentence, which is what gives academic prose its abstract, concept-driven feel.
Watch the same idea move from a verb-based (personal, wordy) form to a noun-based (impersonal, dense) form.
Because the company expanded quickly, it became difficult to manage.
The company's rapid expansion led to management difficulties.
“expanded” becomes “expansion,” “difficult to manage” becomes “management difficulties”; the sentence is shorter and more formal.
The government decided to invest in schools, and this improved literacy.
The government's decision to invest in schools improved literacy.
The whole first clause collapses into a noun phrase that can act as the subject.
The mechanism is a three-step move you can apply on demand: find the action or quality; convert it to its noun; rebuild the sentence around that noun as subject or object.
Turn a “because” clause into a noun subject. “Because pollution increased, health worsened” → “The increase in pollution worsened public health.”
Turn a whole event into the subject of the next sentence, for smooth linking. “The factory closed. This caused unemployment.” → “The closure of the factory caused widespread unemployment.”
Replace “X is important / X is able to” with a noun. “It is important to reduce waste” → “The reduction of waste is a priority.”

This second move (event → subject) is also a cohesion device: naming the previous idea as a noun (“this closure,” “such growth,” “this development”) is a sophisticated way to link paragraphs without cheap connectors like “moreover.”

Nominalisation is powerful, but the failure mode is real: a sentence stuffed with abstract nouns becomes heavy, cold, and hard to read. The Band 9 skill is balance, using nominalisation to raise register while keeping the sentence clear. Two problems recur.

Problem 1 · The noun string. Chaining several abstract nouns with “of” creates an unreadable pile-up.
✗ The implementation of the reduction of the consumption of energy is a necessity.
✓ Reducing energy consumption is essential.

Problem 2 · Losing the doer entirely. Sometimes the reader needs to know who acted; total nominalisation can hide responsibility unhelpfully.
✗ A decision was reached and an implementation followed.
✓ The committee decided to act and then implemented the plan.
The register marker of the top bands

Nominalisation is one of the clearest features that separates a Band 6.5 script (which reads like careful speech) from a Band 8 script (which reads like academic writing). Its two payoffs map directly onto the marking criteria: it lifts Lexical Resource, because it forces precise, formal word choice, and it lifts Coherence and Cohesion, because naming a previous idea as a noun links sentences elegantly. The instruction is to use it deliberately in your topic sentences and transitions, where density and formality matter most, while keeping your explanatory sentences clear.

Skills: Writing
Task 2 topic sentence: The rapid urbanisation of developing nations has placed enormous pressure on public infrastructure.
Task 2 cohesion (event → subject): This expansion, however, has come at a significant environmental cost.
Task 1 summary: The overall growth in exports was matched by a comparable rise in imports.
End of Chapter 9, and of Module 3. Module 4 (The Full Workbook), Chapter 10, follows: full essay editing and speaking transcript polish, then the complete answer keys in Chapter 11.

chapters.title: 9. Practice · Nominalisation & Academic Density
blocks: Nominalisation turns a verb or adjective into a noun -- decide becomes decision, difficult becomes difficulty. Once an idea is a noun it can become the subject of a sentence, which is exactly what gives academic prose its abstract, concept-driven feel.
**Why it matters:** Nominalisation is the single grammatical habit most responsible for the difference between conversational English and academic English.
Nominalisation converts an action word (verb) or a quality word (adjective) into a thing word (noun). Once an idea is a noun, it can become the **subject** of a sentence.

Practising these families in both directions -- spotting the verb form and producing the noun form on demand -- is what makes nominalisation available under exam pressure rather than something you only recognise when reading.

blocks.title: Exercise 9.1 · Nominalisation Drill
blocks.instructions: Rewrite each sentence in a more academic register by nominalising the word in brackets, making the resulting noun the subject or object. One item asks you to simplify an over-nominalised string.

items.prompt: The company expanded rapidly, and this created management problems. (nominalise “expanded”)
items.answer: The company's rapid expansion created management problems.
accepted: The company's rapid expansion created management problems.
items.reason: “expanded” → “expansion” as the subject.

items.prompt: Because the population grew, the demand for housing rose. (nominalise “grew”)
items.answer: The growth of the population raised the demand for housing.
accepted: The growth of the population raised the demand for housing.
Population growth raised the demand for housing.
items.reason: “grew” → “growth” subject.

items.prompt: The factory closed, which caused widespread unemployment. (nominalise “closed”)
items.answer: The closure of the factory caused widespread unemployment.
accepted: The closure of the factory caused widespread unemployment.
items.reason: “closed” → “closure.”

items.prompt: It is important to reduce waste. (nominalise “reduce” and “important”)
items.answer: The reduction of waste is a priority.
accepted: The reduction of waste is a priority.
Waste reduction is important.
items.reason: “reduce” → “reduction”; “important” idea → “priority.”

items.prompt: The government decided to invest in railways, and this improved transport. (nominalise “decided”)
items.answer: The government's decision to invest in railways improved transport.
accepted: The government's decision to invest in railways improved transport.
items.reason: “decided” → “decision.”

items.prompt: Because energy is consumed at a high rate, emissions have risen. (nominalise “consumed”)
items.answer: The high consumption of energy has raised emissions.
accepted: The high consumption of energy has raised emissions.
High energy consumption has raised emissions.
items.reason: “consumed” → “consumption.”

items.prompt: The team failed to plan properly, which led to delays. (nominalise “failed”)
items.answer: The team's failure to plan properly led to delays.
accepted: The team's failure to plan properly led to delays.
items.reason: “failed” → “failure.”

items.prompt: Many species have become extinct, and this worries scientists. (nominalise “become extinct”)
items.answer: The extinction of many species worries scientists.
accepted: The extinction of many species worries scientists.
items.reason: “become extinct” → “extinction.”

items.prompt: The city developed quickly, and this attracted investors. (nominalise “developed”)
items.answer: The city's rapid development attracted investors.
accepted: The city's rapid development attracted investors.
items.reason: “developed” → “development.”

items.prompt: Prices increased sharply, which reduced consumer spending. (nominalise “increased”)
items.answer: The sharp increase in prices reduced consumer spending.
accepted: The sharp increase in prices reduced consumer spending.
items.reason: “increased” → “increase in.”

items.prompt: People are more aware of climate change, and this has changed behaviour. (nominalise “aware”)
items.answer: Growing awareness of climate change has changed behaviour.
accepted: Growing awareness of climate change has changed behaviour.
items.reason: “aware” → “awareness.”

items.prompt: The two countries cooperated, and trade improved. (nominalise “cooperated”)
items.answer: Cooperation between the two countries improved trade.
accepted: Cooperation between the two countries improved trade.
items.reason: “cooperated” → “cooperation.”

items.prompt: Simplify the noun string: The implementation of the reduction of the consumption of energy is a necessity.
items.answer: Reducing energy consumption is essential.
accepted: Reducing energy consumption is essential.
Cutting energy consumption is essential.
items.reason: Break the “of” pile-up back into a clear form.

items.prompt: The scientists analysed the data carefully, and this revealed a pattern. (nominalise “analysed”)
items.answer: The scientists' careful analysis of the data revealed a pattern.
accepted: The scientists' careful analysis of the data revealed a pattern.
items.reason: “analysed” → “analysis.”

items.prompt: Because the roads were poor, transport costs were high. (nominalise “poor”)
items.answer: The poor condition of the roads raised transport costs.
accepted: The poor condition of the roads raised transport costs.
The poor state of the roads raised transport costs.
items.reason: “poor (roads)” → “the poor condition of the roads.”

blocks.title: Exercise 9.2 · Restructuring and De-fogging
blocks.instructions: Added to complete Chapter 9 (every other chapter has two exercises). Items 1–6: rewrite each sentence with the restructuring move in brackets from 9.3. Items 7–10: each sentence is over-nominalised; rewrite it so it stays formal but reads clearly, as in the “Do not over-nominalise into fog” box.

items.prompt: Because traffic increased, air quality in the city declined. (move 1: “because” clause → noun subject)
items.answer: The increase in traffic caused a decline in air quality in the city.
accepted: The increase in traffic caused a decline in air quality in the city.
The increase in traffic led to a decline in the city's air quality.
Increased traffic caused a decline in air quality in the city.
items.reason: The “because” clause becomes the noun subject “the increase in traffic”; “declined” becomes “a decline in”.

items.prompt: Because the region became poorer, crime rose sharply. (move 1)
items.answer: The region's growing poverty led to a sharp rise in crime.
accepted: The region's growing poverty led to a sharp rise in crime.
Growing poverty in the region led to a sharp rise in crime.
The increase in poverty in the region caused a sharp rise in crime.
items.reason: “became poorer” → “poverty” (adjective poor → noun poverty, as in the 9.1 table); “rose” → “a rise in”.

items.prompt: The government banned plastic bags. This reduced litter on beaches. (move 2: event → subject of the next sentence)
items.answer: The government's ban on plastic bags reduced litter on beaches.
accepted: The government's ban on plastic bags reduced litter on beaches.
The ban on plastic bags reduced litter on beaches.
items.reason: The first sentence collapses into the noun phrase “the ban on plastic bags”, which becomes the subject.

items.prompt: Many young people migrated to cities. This weakened rural communities. (move 2)
items.answer: The migration of young people to cities weakened rural communities.
accepted: The migration of young people to cities weakened rural communities.
The large-scale migration of young people to cities weakened rural communities.
items.reason: “migrated” → “the migration of”; the whole event is now the subject.

items.prompt: It is important to protect endangered species. (move 3: “It is important to …” → noun)
items.answer: The protection of endangered species is a priority.
accepted: The protection of endangered species is a priority.
The protection of endangered species is essential.
Protecting endangered species is a priority.
items.reason: “to protect” → “the protection of”, and the vague “important” becomes a precise noun complement (“a priority”).

items.prompt: Many students are not able to afford university fees. (move 3: “be able to” → noun)
items.answer: Many students lack the ability to afford university fees.
accepted: Many students lack the ability to afford university fees.
The inability of many students to afford university fees is a concern.
Many students' inability to afford university fees is a concern.
items.reason: “are not able to” → “lack the ability to” / “inability” (able → ability, as in the 9.1 table).

items.prompt: The implementation of the improvement of the quality of the provision of education is required.
items.answer: Improving the quality of education is necessary.
accepted: Improving the quality of education is necessary.
The quality of education needs to be improved.
Educational quality must be improved.
items.reason: A noun string of four “of” phrases is unreadable; keep one strong idea (quality of education) and use a verb form for the action.

items.prompt: The reduction of the consumption of water by the population of the city is a necessity.
items.answer: The city's population needs to reduce its water consumption.
accepted: The city's population needs to reduce its water consumption.
Reducing water consumption in the city is necessary.
The city needs to reduce its water consumption.
items.reason: Turn one of the stacked nouns back into a verb (reduction → reduce) and replace “of the population of the city” with a possessive.

items.prompt: There was an expansion in the utilisation of the internet by the elderly for the purpose of communication.
items.answer: Older people increasingly use the internet to communicate.
accepted: Older people increasingly use the internet to communicate.
Internet use among older people for communication has expanded.
More elderly people now use the internet to communicate.
items.reason: “utilisation” is an inflated noun for “use”, and “for the purpose of communication” is fog for “to communicate”; formal does not mean wordy.

items.prompt: The occurrence of the failure of the system was a consequence of the lack of maintenance.
items.answer: The system failed because of a lack of maintenance.
accepted: The system failed because of a lack of maintenance.
The system's failure was caused by a lack of maintenance.
A lack of maintenance caused the system to fail.
items.reason: “The occurrence of the failure” adds nothing; keep at most one nominalisation (failure or lack) and let a clear verb carry the cause.

chapters.title: 10. Full Essay Editing & Speaking Transcript Polish
blocks: Integrated self-editing under exam conditions: the six-pass checklist, five full flawed essays to repair from heavily to lightly flawed, and five spoken answers to raise one band without sounding scripted.

In every chapter so far, you fixed one error type at a time, knowing in advance what to look for. A real exam is not like that. In a real essay, every rule from Modules 1 to 3 fires at once, the errors are mixed and unlabelled, and you have to catch your own mistakes under time pressure with no key beside you. This final module trains exactly that skill: integrated self-editing. You will repair whole flawed essays containing the full range of errors, then upgrade real spoken answers from safe-but-basic to controlled-and-flexible.
10.1 How to use this workbook chapter

Each editing task below is a complete flawed essay or paragraph written at roughly Band 5.5 to 6.0, seeded with the specific error types you have studied. Work in a disciplined sequence rather than reading randomly for “things that look wrong.”
The self-editing checklist (run it in this order)
Agreement pass: check every verb against its true subject (Chapter 1).
Tense pass: check that every time frame is correct and consistent (Chapter 2).
Article pass: check every singular noun for a / an / the / zero (Chapter 3).
Preposition pass: check dependent and data prepositions (Chapter 4).
Structure pass: check for fragments, run-ons, and comma splices; look for a variety of complex sentences (Chapter 5).
Range pass: is there at least one passive, one conditional, and some hedging where appropriate (Chapters 6, 7)? Is there one accurate high-band structure (Chapters 8, 9)?
Do a separate pass for each item. Trying to catch everything in one read is how errors slip through; specialists beat generalists when proofreading.

There are five editing essays in the exercise for this chapter, graded from heavily flawed (Essay 1) to lightly flawed (Essay 5). Each has a model corrected version and a breakdown of the errors by category, so you can see which of your six passes would have caught each one. Do them in order; the later essays assume you have internalised the earlier fixes.

You are not rewriting the essay into your own style. You are making the minimum corrections needed for accuracy and range while preserving the writer's meaning. That is exactly what you must do to your own script in the last five minutes of the exam.

Grammar is assessed in Speaking too, under the same Grammatical Range and Accuracy heading, but the target is different: in Speaking you need controlled flexibility in real time, not written density. The five speaking items in the exercise give you a real, basic-but-safe spoken answer and ask you to raise it one band by adding exactly the moves this course has taught, without making it sound scripted.
The upgrade toolkit for Speaking, in order of value:
Fix the base accuracy first: agreement, tense, and articles, since these cost the most.
Add one complex sentence: a because, although, or which clause to connect two ideas.
Add a tense contrast: move between past, present, and future to show range (“I used to … but now I … and I think I'll …”).
Add one hedging phrase: “it depends,” “I'd say,” “on the whole,” “tend to.”
Optionally, one natural cleft for emphasis: “what I really enjoy is …”

The aim is spoken English that is accurate and flexible, not a memorised paragraph. One natural complex sentence and one tense contrast in a Part 2 answer will do more for your score than a rehearsed idiom.
Why integrated editing is the real exam skill

Both writing tasks end with a few minutes that should be spent editing, and candidates who edit systematically routinely gain half a band in Grammatical Range and Accuracy over those who do not, because the same slips (a dropped -s, a missing article, a will in an if-clause) are both common and easy to catch on a targeted pass. In Speaking, the ability to self-correct smoothly (“the number of people were, sorry, was rising”) is itself a positive marker of control. This chapter builds the habit that turns everything you have learned into marks under exam conditions.

Skills: Writing, Speaking
Editing gain: A systematic six-pass edit in the last five minutes typically removes most agreement, tense, and article slips.
Speaking self-correction: “They has - sorry, they have - improved a lot recently.”
The five editing essays and five speaking-polish items are in the exercises for this chapter. Chapter 11 then gives the complete, step-by-step answer keys for every exercise in the book.

chapters.title: 10. Practice · Full Essay Editing & Speaking Transcript Polish
blocks: Trying to catch every grammar error in one read is how mistakes slip through. Run a separate, single-focus pass for each rule -- agreement, then tense, then articles, then prepositions -- because specialists beat generalists when proofreading.
**Why it matters:** This is the checklist that ties every earlier chapter together into a single, repeatable editing routine you can run on any essay before you submit it.
1. **Agreement pass** -- check every verb against its true subject (Chapter 1).
2. **Tense pass** -- check that every time frame is correct and consistent (Chapter 2).
3. **Article pass** -- check every singular noun for a/an/the/zero (Chapter 3).
4. **Preposition pass** -- check dependent and data prepositions (Chapter 4).

Do a **separate pass for each item** rather than trying to catch everything in one read-through. Specialists beat generalists when proofreading -- a single-focus pass catches errors a general read-through misses entirely.

blocks.title: Exercise 10.1 · Full Essay Editing
blocks.instructions: Five flawed essays, graded from heavily to lightly flawed. Run the six-pass checklist on each and rewrite it correctly, preserving the writer's meaning. Essay 5 also asks you to add one high-band structure.

items.prompt: EDIT ESSAY 1 (heavily flawed). Correct every error, preserving the meaning. “In many country, the number of student who go abroad for study have increased in recent years. This trend have both advantage and disadvantage. On one hand, student who studies in foreign university gets access to better facility and they can learns new culture. On other hand, it is very expensive and many family cannot affords it. In my opinion, if government will provide more scholarship, this problem can be solved. According to me, the advantage is more than the disadvantage.”
items.answer: In many countries, the number of students who go abroad to study has increased in recent years. This trend has both advantages and disadvantages. On the one hand, students who study at foreign universities gain access to better facilities and can learn about new cultures. On the other hand, it is very expensive, and many families cannot afford it. In my opinion, if the government provided more scholarships, this problem could be solved. Overall, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.
accepted: In many countries, the number of students who go abroad to study has increased in recent years. This trend has both advantages and disadvantages. On the one hand, students who study at foreign universities gain access to better facilities and can learn about new cultures. On the other hand, it is very expensive, and many families cannot afford it. In my opinion, if the government provided more scholarships, this problem could be solved. Overall, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.
items.reason: Agreement: country→countries, student→students, have→has (the number is singular), studies→study, gets→gain, learns→learn, affords→afford. Articles: on the one hand, on the other hand, the government. Conditional: “if government will provide”→“if the government provided … could be solved” (no will in the if-clause). Register: “According to me”→“Overall / In my view”; “advantage is more than”→“advantages outweigh the disadvantages.”

items.prompt: EDIT ESSAY 2. Correct every error. “Nowadays, technology have changed the way we communicate. In the past, people was writing letters which take many days to arrive. But now, we can sends a message in a second. Although this is convenient, but it also have some negative effect. For example, many young people spends too much time on their phone and they forgets how to talk face to face. If this trend continue, our social skill will became weaker.”
items.answer: Nowadays, technology has changed the way we communicate. In the past, people wrote letters, which took many days to arrive. Now, however, we can send a message in a second. Although this is convenient, it also has some negative effects. For example, many young people spend too much time on their phones and forget how to talk face to face. If this trend continues, our social skills will become weaker.
accepted: Nowadays, technology has changed the way we communicate. In the past, people wrote letters, which took many days to arrive. Now, however, we can send a message in a second. Although this is convenient, it also has some negative effects. For example, many young people spend too much time on their phones and forget how to talk face to face. If this trend continues, our social skills will become weaker.
items.reason: Agreement: have→has, can sends→send, have→has, spends→spend, forgets→forget, skill→skills. Tense: “was writing”→“wrote” (a past habit), “take”→“took.” Structure: “Although … but” is a double connector - drop “but.” Conditional: “if … continue … will became”→“continues … will become” (base verb after will). Plurals/articles: effect→effects, phone→phones.

items.prompt: EDIT ESSAY 3. Correct every error. “Pollution is one of the most serious problem in the world today. The main cause of it are the vehicles and the factories. In big cities, the air quality have become very poor, and many people suffers from breathing disease. Government should took strong action. If they had acted earlier, the situation would not be so bad now. It is high time we do something about this issue.”
items.answer: Pollution is one of the most serious problems in the world today. The main causes of it are vehicles and factories. In big cities, air quality has become very poor, and many people suffer from breathing diseases. Governments should take strong action. If they had acted earlier, the situation would not be so bad now. It is high time we did something about this issue.
accepted: Pollution is one of the most serious problems in the world today. The main causes of it are vehicles and factories. In big cities, air quality has become very poor, and many people suffer from breathing diseases. Governments should take strong action. If they had acted earlier, the situation would not be so bad now. It is high time we did something about this issue.
items.reason: Agreement: problem→problems (after “one of the most”), cause … are→causes are, have become→has become (subject “quality”), suffers→suffer, disease→diseases. Verb form: “should took”→“should take.” Articles: “the vehicles and the factories”→general “vehicles and factories”; “Government”→“Governments.” Mixed conditional is already correct (“had acted … would not be … now”). “It is high time” takes the past subjunctive: “we did,” not “we do.”

items.prompt: EDIT ESSAY 4 (lightly flawed). Correct every error. “There is many reasons why people choose to live in cities. Firstly, cities offers more job opportunities than rural areas. Secondly, the access to good education and healthcare are better. However, urban life also have its drawbacks, such as pollution and high cost of living. Despite of these problems, the majority of people still prefers city life.”
items.answer: There are many reasons why people choose to live in cities. Firstly, cities offer more job opportunities than rural areas. Secondly, access to good education and healthcare is better. However, urban life also has its drawbacks, such as pollution and a high cost of living. Despite these problems, the majority of people still prefer city life.
accepted: There are many reasons why people choose to live in cities. Firstly, cities offer more job opportunities than rural areas. Secondly, access to good education and healthcare is better. However, urban life also has its drawbacks, such as pollution and a high cost of living. Despite these problems, the majority of people still prefer city life.
items.reason: Agreement: “There is many”→“There are many,” offers→offer, “access … are”→“access … is” (subject is “access,” singular), have→has, prefers→prefer (subject “majority of people” treated as plural here). Preposition: “Despite of”→“Despite” (no “of”). Article: “a high cost of living.”

items.prompt: EDIT ESSAY 5 (subtle errors + one range upgrade). Correct the errors, then add ONE high-band structure (an inversion, a cleft, or a nominalisation) where it fits. “Renewable energy has become more important in recent years. Many governments have invested in solar and wind power because they want to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels. This is a positive development, but it is also expensive. Not only it reduces emissions, it also creates jobs. The transition will take time, but it is necessary.”
items.answer: Renewable energy has become increasingly important in recent years. Many governments have invested in solar and wind power because they want to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels. This shift is a positive development, though a costly one. Not only does it reduce emissions, but it also creates jobs. The transition to clean energy will take time, but it is necessary.
accepted: Renewable energy has become increasingly important in recent years. Many governments have invested in solar and wind power because they want to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels. This shift is a positive development, though a costly one. Not only does it reduce emissions, but it also creates jobs. The transition to clean energy will take time, but it is necessary.
items.reason: The base text is nearly accurate; the key fix is the inversion: “Not only it reduces”→“Not only does it reduce …, but it also creates” (question word order after the fronted “not only”). Optional upgrades shown: “increasingly important” for register, “This shift” as a nominalised cohesive subject, “the transition to clean energy” for density.

blocks: Speaking is graded on the same Grammatical Range and Accuracy criterion as Writing, but the target is different: controlled flexibility in real time, not written density. Fix base accuracy first, then add one complex sentence and one tense contrast.
**Why it matters:** Candidates often over-prepare Writing grammar and under-prepare the same criterion for Speaking, where the goal is different.
The upgrade toolkit for Speaking, in order of value
1. **Fix base accuracy first** -- agreement, tense, and articles, since these cost the most.
2. **Add one complex sentence** -- a because, although, or which clause to connect two ideas.
3. **Add a tense contrast** -- move between past, present, and future to show range: I used to..., but now I...
Accurate, flexible spoken English -- not a memorised paragraph. One natural complex sentence and one tense contrast in a Part 2 answer will do more for your score than a rehearsed idiom.

blocks.title: Exercise 10.2 · Speaking Transcript Polish
blocks.instructions: Five basic-but-safe spoken answers. Raise each one band by fixing the base accuracy and adding a complex sentence, a tense contrast, and a hedging phrase, without making it sound scripted.

items.prompt: SPEAKING POLISH 1. Raise this Part 1 answer one band, keeping it natural. “Yes, I like reading. I read many book. My favourite is story book. I read every day because it is relaxing.”
items.answer: Yes, I really enjoy reading. I read a lot of books, and my favourite genre is fiction. I try to read every day because I find it relaxing, and I'd say it's the best way for me to unwind after work.
accepted: Yes, I really enjoy reading. I read a lot of books, and my favourite genre is fiction. I try to read every day because I find it relaxing, and I'd say it's the best way for me to unwind after work.
items.reason: Fix: “many book”→“a lot of books,” “story book”→“fiction.” Add range: a because clause, a hedging phrase (“I'd say”), and a cleft-like emphasis (“it's the best way … to unwind”), plus a tense/register lift.

items.prompt: SPEAKING POLISH 2. Raise this Part 1 answer one band. “I live in Dhaka. It is big city. There is many people. I like it because my family is here.”
items.answer: I live in Dhaka, which is a very large and crowded city. Although there are a lot of people and the traffic can be difficult, I really like living here because my whole family is nearby.
accepted: I live in Dhaka, which is a very large and crowded city. Although there are a lot of people and the traffic can be difficult, I really like living here because my whole family is nearby.
items.reason: Fix: “big city”→“a very large … city,” “There is many”→“there are a lot of.” Add range: a relative clause (“which is …”), a contrast clause (“Although …”), and a reason clause (“because …”).

items.prompt: SPEAKING POLISH 3. Raise this Part 2 answer one band. “I want to talk about my phone. I use it every day. It is very useful. I use it for call and internet. I cannot live without it.”
items.answer: The possession I'd like to talk about is my phone, which I use constantly throughout the day. I rely on it for almost everything, from making calls to browsing the internet, and honestly I'm not sure how I'd manage without it now.
accepted: The possession I'd like to talk about is my phone, which I use constantly throughout the day. I rely on it for almost everything, from making calls to browsing the internet, and honestly I'm not sure how I'd manage without it now.
items.reason: Fix: “for call”→“for making calls.” Add range: a cleft opener (“The possession I'd like to talk about is …”), a relative clause, a hedging phrase (“honestly … I'm not sure”), and a conditional touch (“how I'd manage without it”).

items.prompt: SPEAKING POLISH 4. Raise this Part 3 answer one band. “Yes, technology changed our life. Before, people did everything by hand. Now, machine do the work. I think it is good.”
items.answer: Yes, technology has changed our lives enormously. Whereas people used to do almost everything by hand, machines now handle much of the work, which has made life far more efficient. On the whole, I'd say the change has been positive, though it does have some downsides.
accepted: Yes, technology has changed our lives enormously. Whereas people used to do almost everything by hand, machines now handle much of the work, which has made life far more efficient. On the whole, I'd say the change has been positive, though it does have some downsides.
items.reason: Fix: “changed”→“has changed,” “life”→“lives,” “machine do”→“machines … handle.” Add range: a contrast clause (“Whereas … used to …”), a tense contrast (past habit vs present), hedging (“On the whole, I'd say”), and a concession (“though it does have …”).

items.prompt: SPEAKING POLISH 5. Raise this Part 3 answer one band. “Government should help poor people. They can give money and job. If they do this, poverty will reduce.”
items.answer: I think governments have a real responsibility to support people living in poverty, for instance by providing financial assistance and creating job opportunities. If such measures were implemented effectively, poverty would be likely to fall, although it clearly cannot be solved overnight.
accepted: I think governments have a real responsibility to support people living in poverty, for instance by providing financial assistance and creating job opportunities. If such measures were implemented effectively, poverty would be likely to fall, although it clearly cannot be solved overnight.
items.reason: Fix: “Government”→“governments,” “poor people”→“people living in poverty,” “give money and job”→“providing financial assistance and creating job opportunities.” Add range: a second conditional (“If … were implemented … would be likely to fall”), hedging (“be likely to”), and a concession clause.

chapters.title: 11. Answer Keys, Diagnostic Index & Exam Routine
blocks: A consolidation reference rather than new drills: how to review a wrong answer, a diagnostic index of the highest-frequency errors with the single rule that fixes each, the full chapter map, and the ten-minute exam self-edit routine.

Every exercise in this course is self-checking: when you submit an answer, the platform shows you the correct version, the reason it is correct, and a Bengali note explaining the underlying rule. This final chapter is not another set of drills. It is a consolidation reference, the place to come back to when a mistake recurs, so you can find the one rule that fixes a whole family of errors. Use it as a diagnostic index: identify the error you keep making, then re-read the rule and the chapter it comes from.
11.1 How to review an incorrect answer
When you get an item wrong, do not simply read the correct answer and move on. Spend thirty seconds diagnosing it, because the same error type will return in your own writing.
Read the model answer and the reason together, so you see the rule in action, not just the fix.
Name the error type: is it agreement, tense, article, preposition, structure, or a range issue?
Go back to the source chapter for that type (the map is in 11.3) and re-read the one rule that governs it.
Write two fresh sentences of your own that apply the rule correctly. Producing the form, not just recognising it, is what moves it into your active grammar.
11.2 The highest-frequency errors, and the single rule that fixes each
These are the mistakes that appear most often in Bangladeshi scripts. If you internalise this short table, you remove the majority of your recurring errors.
The verb agrees with the true subject, not the nearest noun.
Uncountable nouns take no a/an and no plural.
A finished year takes the past simple, not the present perfect.
‘Since/for’ take a perfect tense, not the present continuous.
Direct-translation prepositions: discuss X; in my opinion.
A dependent clause cannot stand alone (fragment).
Two clauses need more than a comma (comma splice).
Hedge sweeping claims: may, tend to, generally.
After a fronted negative, use question word order.
verb–subject matching, the eight tricky cases
the twelve tenses; past simple vs present perfect; simple vs continuous
time/place/data prepositions; dependent prepositions; L1 fixes
clauses; adverbial and relative clauses; fragments/run-ons/splices
passive across tenses; impersonal frames; process writing
the four conditionals; the if-clause rule; hedging toolkit
verb/adjective → noun; academic density and cohesion
the six-pass self-edit; raising spoken answers one band

On exam day, the grammar you have built pays off only if you leave time to apply the self-edit. Reserve the last few minutes of each writing task for a targeted review, running the passes from Chapter 10 in order.

Task 1 (leave ~3 minutes): check every tense against the time frame of the data; check the data prepositions (by, from, to, of); check that “the number of” and “the proportion of” take singular verbs.

Task 2 (leave ~5 minutes): run agreement, article, and preposition passes; confirm no “will” sits in an if-clause; confirm you have a variety of complex sentences and at least one clean high-band structure.
Speaking (in real time): if you hear an agreement or tense slip, self-correct smoothly and move on; a clean self-correction is a sign of control, not weakness.

Knowing a rule and applying it under pressure are different skills, and the gap between them is closed only by the review habit this chapter describes. Candidates who diagnose their recurring errors, return to the governing rule, and then produce fresh correct examples improve far faster than those who only complete drills once. Treat every wrong answer in this course as information about which single rule to revisit. That loop, error to rule to fresh production, is what turns study into a higher band.

Skills: Writing, Speaking
Review loop: Wrong answer → name the error type → re-read the rule → write two correct sentences of your own.
Exam routine: Always reserve the final minutes to run the six editing passes in order.

This completes the course. Return to any chapter's exercises to practise until the correct forms feel automatic; the platform will keep scoring you and showing the reason and Bengali note for every item.
